title: Fair-FedMOE: Group-Fair One-Shot Federated Learning via Prototype-Guided Experts for Medical Imaging Analysis
claim: Fine-tuned foundation models show large subgroup performance gaps, and naively averaging divergent local models in one-shot federated learning produces a degraded global model.
layout: 2 stacked panels: top bar charts, bottom left-to-right federated flow diagram
description: The figure has two stacked panels. Panel (a), "Subgroup Performance Disparity", has two charts. On the left is a grouped bar chart of overall AUC for RETFound and DINOv3, comparing linear probe (gray) with fine-tuned (blue for RETFound, red for DINOv3). On the right is a horizontal bar chart of subgroup AUC for six age and sex groups. Red and blue bars are paired, and the best and worst values are annotated, e.g. 0.955 and 0.759. A callout box gives the performance gaps, RETFound Δ=0.172 and DINOv3 Δ=0.145. Panel (b), "Model Inconsistency", is a left-to-right diagram. Hospital icons for Client 1 and Client k, each with retinal fundus images, feed red and blue local models θ1 and θk. Arrows carry these to a cloud server icon, with the weighted-average formula θ_avg above it. A gray arrow leads to a gray degraded global model and a red declining bar chart, labeled "Poor Performance".
caption: Fairness challenges in OFL fine-tuning of medical FMs. (a) Subgroup Performance Disparity: Both retinal-specific and general-purpose FMs show significant performance gaps across subgroups. (b) Model Inconsistency: Data heterogeneity causes local models to diverge. Naive weighted averaging introduces parameter conflicts and degrades global model performance.
abstract: Group fairness can ensure equitable performance across different demographic subgroups for medical image analysis. However, the current fine-tuned foundation models (FMs) exhibit significant subgroup disparity. One-shot federated learning (OFL) can potentially mitigate this by leveraging cross-institutional data diversity within a single communication round. However, heterogeneous distributions across medical institutions may cause OFL local models to diverge severely, resulting in parameter conflicts that amplify disparity upon aggregation. To address these challenges, we propose Fair-FedMOE, a group-fair OFL framework for medical FMs. During local training, Fairness-aware Expert Routing leverages learnable prototypes to route samples to group-specific experts, enabling subgroup-specialized learning to capture group-specific features without inter-group interference. During model aggregation, Prototype-guided Differential Aggregation computes personalized weights based on prototype similarity and applies differentiated aggregation strategies to filter conflicting updates. We propose RES-AUC, a Rawlsian justice-inspired metric based on worst-group performance that remains stable as groups increase. Extensive experiments on retinal and chest X-ray datasets with multiple FMs demonstrate consistent fairness gains without sacrificing accuracy.
